title: Sowing the Wind, Reaping the Whirlwind
summary: An alarm sounds: an eagle hovers over the LORD's house because Israel has broken his covenant. The people claim to know God, but they have made kings without him and idols with their silver, including the calf of Samaria, which a craftsman made and which will be smashed. They have sown the wind and will reap the whirlwind; they have hired lovers among the nations, multiplied altars for sinning, and forgotten their Maker, so they will return to Egypt.
story: Chapter 7 pictured Israel's political chaos. Chapter 8 names its two root causes side by side: kings made without God and idols made with human hands. The chapter reads like a summary of the whole case against the northern kingdom from its beginning, since both its kingship and its calf worship go back to its founding under Jeroboam I. The announcement that Israel will return to Egypt, a reversal of the exodus, becomes a recurring threat in the chapters that follow (9:3; 11:5).
historical:
When the northern tribes broke from Judah after Solomon's death, around 930 BC, they made Jeroboam I their king. To keep his people from worshiping in Jerusalem, Jeroboam set up two golden calves, one at Bethel and one at Dan, and told the people that these were the gods who brought them up out of Egypt (1 Kings 12:26-30), words echoing Aaron's calf at Sinai (Exodus 32:4). The calf of Samaria (verses 5-6) probably refers to the Bethel calf as the national shrine of the kingdom whose capital was Samaria, though some think a calf stood in Samaria itself. Many scholars think the calves were meant as pedestals on which the invisible LORD stood, as the cherubim were his throne in Jerusalem; Hosea's point is that, whatever their intention, they had become idols.

They set up kings, but not by Me (verse 4) fits the years after 753 BC, when kings seized power by assassination, but it may also look back to the kingdom's origin. Hired lovers among the nations (verses 9-10) refers to tribute paid to Assyria, beginning with Menahem, who raised a thousand talents of silver from Israel's wealthy men to pay Tiglath-pileser III (2 Kings 15:19-20). The king of princes (verse 10) may be a play on the Assyrian royal title king of kings. The fire sent on the cities and citadels was fulfilled in the Assyrian campaigns culminating in 722 BC and, for Judah's fortified cities, in Sennacherib's invasion of 701 BC.
cultural:
The ram's horn (shofar) was blown to warn a city of approaching enemies. The eagle of verse 1 translates a word that also covers the vulture, and either sense works: a bird of prey circling over its victim. The house of the LORD probably means the land and people of Israel, God's household, rather than a temple building.

The proverb of verse 7, sow the wind and reap the whirlwind, draws on the farming year, in which what is sown determines what is harvested. Wind stands for what is empty and worthless; the whirlwind is the same emptiness returned with destructive force. Altars multiplied across the land (verse 11) show a religion growing in quantity while decaying in faithfulness. The great things of My law written for Israel (verse 12) refers to instruction God had given in writing, which the people now treated as foreign to them. The return to Egypt (verse 13) is a symbolic threat: the redeemed people will be sent back into slavery, whether literally in Egypt or in the new Egypt of Assyria (see 9:3; 11:5).
literary: The chapter opens with an alarm and then moves in quick, loosely connected sayings, each with its own image. It pairs the two great charges against Israel in verse 4, kings and idols, and develops each. Irony is everywhere. Israel cries, O our God, we know You, but has rejected good. The calf is from Israel, a craftsman made it, and it is not God. Ephraim multiplied altars for sin, and they became altars for sinning. Israel has hired lovers, reversing the usual image of a prostitute who is paid; here Israel pays. Sound play strengthens the sayings: in Hebrew, the words for what sprouts and for flour in verse 7 rhyme (tsemach and qemach).

outline.t: The alarm: covenant broken, the enemy pursues
Kings without God and the calf of Samaria
Sowing the wind; hired lovers among the nations
Altars for sinning; Israel has forgotten his Maker

doctrines.note: A craftsman made it, and it is not God (verse 6). Idols are human products, and people who worship them become like them, empty and worthless. The calf may have been intended to honor the LORD, but a God shaped by human hands is not the living God.
The alarm sounds because the people have transgressed My covenant and rebelled against My law (verse 1). The covenant had terms, and Israel's disasters are the covenant's own consequences.
They sow the wind and reap the whirlwind. Judgment often takes the form of sin's own consequences, multiplied: empty trust returns as destruction.
They set up kings, but not by Me. Israel's kingship was meant to be under God's rule. When rulers are made by conspiracy and power alone, the kingdom cannot stand.

words.note: Egel, a calf or young bull. The bull was a symbol of strength and fertility in the ancient Near East, associated with gods including Baal. The word recalls both Aaron's calf at Sinai and Jeroboam's calves. Hosea's scorn, that calf of Samaria, echoes throughout the book (10:5; 13:2).

Zara, to sow. The proverb they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind uses the certainty of the harvest for the certainty of judgment. Elsewhere Hosea uses sowing for blessing (2:23) and calls Israel to sow righteousness (10:12).

Tanah, to hire or pay a fee. Ephraim has hired lovers (verse 9), paying foreign powers for protection. The image reverses the usual picture of prostitution: Israel is the one paying, the ultimate humiliation.

Shakach, to forget. Israel has forgotten his Maker (verse 14). In the Bible, forgetting God is not a lapse of memory but a practical denial of him, living as though he did not exist, which Deuteronomy 8:11-14 warned would happen in prosperity.

christ: The chapter's sharpest charge, they set up kings, but not by Me, sets up the Bible's longing for a king chosen by God. The New Testament proclaims Jesus as that king, anointed by God and not by human conspiracy, who explicitly refused to be made king by force (John 6:15). The proverb of sowing and reaping is also taken up in the New Testament: whatever a man sows, he will reap, and the one who sows to the flesh reaps corruption, while the one who sows to the Spirit reaps eternal life (Galatians 6:7-8). Most deeply, Israel's forgetting of its Maker is answered in the gospel by the God who does not forget his people, who in Christ comes to seek and save the lost (Luke 19:10). These are thematic connections rather than predictions.

hard.q: Was the calf at Bethel meant to be an image of the LORD or of another god?
hard.a:
Jeroboam I presented the calves as the gods who brought Israel out of Egypt (1 Kings 12:28), which suggests they were connected with the worship of the LORD rather than a foreign god, even though the plural wording echoes Aaron's calf at Sinai. Many scholars think the calves were not intended as images of God himself but as pedestals on which the invisible LORD was thought to stand, similar to the role of the cherubim above the ark in Jerusalem. Others think the calves were understood as representations of the LORD, a violation of the second commandment, or that they drew on symbols associated with Baal or the storm god and so blurred the line between the LORD and other gods.

Hosea's judgment does not depend on settling the question. Whatever the calves were meant to be, they had become objects of devotion in their own right (13:2), made by craftsmen and credited with divine power. The prophet's charge is that a religion can keep the LORD's name while its practice has become idolatry.

questions: Israel cried, O our God, we know You, while its life denied it. How can people claim to know God while forgetting him in practice?
They set up kings, but not by Me. In what areas of life do you make decisions without seeking God's direction?
What have you seen of the principle that people reap what they sow, for good or ill?
